stem: Corn output more than doubled, yet many small farmers grew poorer. Who gained most from the rising output?

stimulus.source_note: United States corn production, in millions of bushels, from the National Bureau of Economic Research Macrohistory Database (series A01023USA391NNBR), via FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Public data.
stimulus.text:
United States corn production, in millions of bushels:

| Year | Corn produced |
| 1870 | 1,125 |
| 1880 | 1,707 |
| 1890 | 1,650 |
| 1900 | 2,662 |

options.text: Small farmers, who sold the most corn and kept the profits
options.misconception: Background: small farmers sold less, not more; falling prices and costly machines squeezed them, while large farms sold in volume.

options.text: Large mechanized farms, and the railroads and dealers who moved the crop
The federal government, which collected a tax on every bushel shipped east
options.misconception: Background: the federal government levied no tax on bushels of corn shipped east.

options.text: Foreign buyers overseas, who paid the highest prices for American corn
options.misconception: Background: foreign buyers bought at falling world prices; they did not pay the highest prices.

rationales.A: Background: small farmers sold less, not more; falling prices and costly machines squeezed them, while large farms sold in volume.
rationales.B: Background from the books: large farms could afford the machines that raised output, so they sold the most grain; railroads and grain dealers took their cut moving it east. The gains went to scale and to middlemen, not to the small farmer.
rationales.C: Background: the federal government levied no tax on bushels of corn shipped east.
rationales.D: Background: foreign buyers bought at falling world prices; they did not pay the highest prices.
rationales.general:
Ask who the rising output paid.
1. Read the table. Corn output more than doubles, from 1,125 million bushels in 1870 to 2,662 million in 1900.
2. Background: large farms could afford the machines behind that rise, so they sold the most grain.
3. Background: railroads and grain dealers took their cut moving the crop east, while small farmers sold little at falling prices.
Remember: when output rises, ask who sells the most, because the gains follow scale.
